To use demonstrative pronouns: celui, celle, ceux, celles (+ -ci / -là).
To use celui qui / celle que / ceux de to avoid repetition.
To use possessive pronouns: le mien, la tienne, les siens, le nôtre, les leurs.
Not to confuse the possessive adjective (mon, ma) with the pronoun (le mien).
To shop for clothes and compare.
Saturday, 7 March. Ioana, Madame Bernard and Brigitte (Julien’s mother, who has come from Annecy) are in a bridal shop in the Presqu’île. Elena is on video, on Ioana’s phone.
Good morning, ladies! What date are you looking for a dress for?
For 3 May. I’d like something simple. Not too long, because it’s at the town hall.
Very good. I have three that you might like. This one, in silk, that one, in lace, and the one at the back, more modern.
Oh, the lace one is gorgeous! It looks like mine. I got married in lace, in 1990.
Mine was much simpler. A little white dress, sewn by my mother. Henri used to say it was the most beautiful in Marseille.
Mum, can you see properly? Which one do you prefer?
(on the phone) Show me this one… no, the one on the left. Yes! The silk one really suits you with your hair.
Can I try on the silk one and the lace one?
Of course. The fitting room is over there. Take your time.
(while Ioana is changing) And what about Julien? Does he have a suit? His is too old, he bought it for his cousin’s wedding ten years ago.
I’ve kept Henri’s. It’s navy blue, very elegant. They’re about the same size…
Henri’s suit? You would do that? It would be such a beautiful symbol…
(she comes out of the fitting room, in silk) Well? This one?
(silence, then crying) Oh, Ioana… That’s the one. Stop looking.
She’s right. It’s yours. I can see it in your eyes.
And in the village, in the summer? Will you wear the same one?
No! For the church, Granny has a surprise. But I’m not saying anything. It’s her surprise, not mine.
“Luh myẽ” (nasal) / “la myen” (not nasal, with the n pronounced). Likewise: tien / tienne, sien / sienne.
The pronoun “le nôtre” has a long, closed ô: “luh nohtr”. The adjective “notre” has a short, open o: “notr”.
They replace a noun already mentioned, so you don’t repeat it: “Celle-ci ou celle-là ?” (this dress or that one?). They agree with the noun:
They never stand alone. They are followed by -ci / -là, by qui / que / dont or by “de”:
This one is in silk, that one in lace.
Those who want to come are welcome.
-ci = here, near; -là = there, further away. In everyday speech French people often use “celui-là” for both.
They replace “possessive adjective + noun”: “ma robe” → “la mienne”. They agree with the OBJECT owned, not with the owner:

“Le sien” = his OR hers. Only the gender of the object matters: “le costume de Julien” → “le sien”; “la robe d’Ioana” → “la sienne”. Unlike English, where “his” and “hers” depend on the owner, French only cares about the thing owned.
With “à” and “de”, the article contracts: “Je pense au mien” (à + le mien), “Je parle des miens” (de + les miens). Also: “C’est à moi” = it’s mine (ownership), simpler than “c’est le mien”.
4. Lequel, laquelle: the question of choice
To ask “which one(s)?”, French uses lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles:
There are three dresses. Which one do you prefer?
Which of these suits is the most elegant?

The following Sunday, Madame Bernard invited Julien up to her flat. On her bed there was a big black garment bag. She opened it carefully, the way you open a treasure.
Inside there was a navy-blue suit, with a white shirt and a dark red tie. “It was his,” she said. “Henri bought it for our daughter’s wedding, in 1998. He only wore it twice.”
Julien hesitated. “Madame Bernard, I don’t know if I can… It’s your husband’s suit. It’s not mine.”
“That’s exactly why, my boy. A suit that stays in a wardrobe doesn’t belong to anyone any more. I’d rather it were yours, and that it danced once more. Go on, try it on.”
Julien went into the bathroom to change. The jacket was a little wide at the shoulders, and the trousers a little long. Henri had been taller than him. But the colour suited him very well.

When he came back into the bedroom, Madame Bernard put her hand over her mouth. For a moment she said nothing. Then she smiled. “The tailor on rue Royale can shorten the trousers. For the shoulders, you’ll have to eat more sarmale.”
Julien put his hands in the jacket pockets, to see. In the inside pocket, his fingers touched something. A little piece of paper, folded in four, very old and very soft.
He took it out and unfolded it. It wasn’t paper. It was a tiny black-and-white photo. A young girl sitting on a bench, in front of a café. She was laughing, her hair blowing in the wind.
On the back of the photo, a few words written in pencil, almost faded: “H., place de la Croix-Rousse, Thursday 3 May 1962.”

Julien said nothing. He held the photo out to Madame Bernard. She put on her glasses. She looked for a long time at the laughing girl. Then she looked at the bench, and at the café behind it, Lucette’s.
“For fifty years,” she said softly, “he kept this photo on him. Even at our daughter’s wedding. And I never knew.”
Julien was afraid she would be hurt. But Madame Bernard wasn’t angry. She was surprisingly calm, almost relieved.

“You know, Julien, everyone has their secrets. I had mine too. Henri gave me fifty years of his life, and they’re the most beautiful years of mine. This photo was the little corner of his heart that stayed in Lyon. I’m not going to be jealous of a twenty-year-old girl.”
She put the photo back in Julien’s hand. “This photo isn’t mine. It’s hers. It belongs to Hélène. You’ll give it to her on Wednesday, from me.”

The next day, Julien took the suit to the tailor on rue Royale, an elderly gentleman called Ferrand. He examined the jacket with admiration. “This suit? It belonged to a man who knew how to dress. Today’s suits aren’t as well made as the ones from that time.”

When Julien explained that it was for a wedding, and told him Henri’s story, the old tailor refused to be paid. “For a suit like this one, and for a story like yours, I’m the one who should thank you.”

The following Wednesday, at the care home, Hélène looked at the photo for long minutes. “I remember that day,” she murmured. “He said to me: ‘Don’t move, I want to keep your laugh forever.’ I thought it was just something young men say.”
She smiled, and Julien saw on the old lady’s face exactly the same laugh as in the photo. Sixty-five years later, it was still there.
Before Julien left, Hélène said to him: “Thank Madame Bernard for me. And tell her too that I’d like to see her alone, just the two of us. We have things to say to each other. Things that are ours.”
That evening, Julien hung Henri’s suit in his wardrobe, next to his own. The old one and the new one, side by side, like two friends waiting for the same day.

Reading text: The parcel from Iași
At the end of March, Ioana receives a parcel from her grandmother. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
At the end of March, a big parcel arrived from Romania. On the package was the grandmother’s shaky handwriting: “For Ioana. For the church.”
Inside there was a white blouse, embroidered by hand with red and black thread. And a letter, translated by Elena.
“This blouse is the one I wore at my wedding, in 1966. My mother embroidered it, over a whole winter.”
“Elena didn’t wear it: hers was a modern dress, from the city. But I think that now this blouse belongs to you. It’s yours.”
“The patterns are those of our village. Every village has its own. These mean: the sun, the tree of life and the protection of the family.”
Ioana tried the blouse on in front of the mirror. It fitted her perfectly, as if it had been made for her.
Julien looked at her for a long time. “You know,” he said, “Matisse painted a blouse like that one. But yours is more beautiful.”
